column3: It closely repeats the forgotten meeting, reciprocal abandonment, fire, and lack of helpers.
It frames heedless diversion as continuing until the appointed day of encounter.
Its tasting motif marks experiential consequence, though not the focus ayah's punitive recompense.
It directly joins tasting everlasting punishment to recompense for what people earned.
The same-surah account of patient, certain leaders supplies only broad guidance context.
Remembering the Lord after forgetting provides a constructive counterpart to culpable neglect.
It commands tasting punishment because of disbelief, matching the focus ayah's embodied requital.
The imperative to taste punishment turns rejected warnings into experienced consequence.
It links tasted harm to wrongful conduct, paralleling punishment as a consequence of deeds.
It nearly repeats forgetting the meeting day and the resulting reciprocal abandonment.
The description of human progeny from humble water does not clarify the focus ayah.
It explicitly answers forgotten signs with being forgotten on the Day.
Recognition of truth at the fire is followed by the command to taste punishment for disbelief.
The desire to secure permanence through construction illuminates the focus ayah's everlasting outcome.

The rejected truth is confessed at encounter and followed by tasting punishment for disbelief.
It denies bodily immortality, giving a finite-life contrast to everlasting punishment.
Taste, death, final recompense, fire, and paradise form a broad eschatological parallel.
It directly commands the inhabitants of the fire to taste its burning punishment.
Its ambiguous reference to meeting Moses or the Book only distantly relates to the final encounter.
It depicts an enduring stay in Hell, supporting the permanence element of the punishment.
At death the disbelievers are commanded to taste the punishment of burning.
It leaves opponents until they meet their appointed devastating day.
The rejected contrast reading does not provide positive support for the focus ayah.
Enjoyment of food and drink as reward is too general a contrast to clarify the focus.
The water-driven crop scene does not materially explain forgetting, encounter, or punishment.
False partners are exposed in direct confrontation, illustrating the collapse of claims at encounter.
Messengers warn of the very meeting day later acknowledged by those addressed.
Entering Hell to remain there makes the focus ayah's everlasting punishment concrete.
Its enduring punishment under divine will supports the duration of the focus ayah's penalty.
Reward for deeds offers only a general positive contrast to punishment for deeds.
The nearby lesser punishment is tasted before the greater one so that people might return.
Those who do not expect encounter demand to see God, exposing their refusal of its proper terms.
It names the promised day as an actual encounter, though for the protected rather than punished.
It plainly depicts criminals abiding permanently in the punishment of Hell.
It names the greater punishment as the result after turning away and disbelieving.
The warned meeting day becomes the realized arrival at Hell and the due punishment.
Destroyed generations are a general warning sign but do not develop the focus ayah's mechanism.
It directly commands tasting punishment because of disbelief.
Ignored warning, a rejected request to return, and the command to taste form a close consequence pattern.
Its doubt about the Hour supplies the denial that the focus ayah brings to realized encounter.
Eternal residence in fire is relevant but gives little account of forgetting or tasting.
Inheritance of paradise by deeds is only a broad reward-side contrast.
The same-surah assertion of revelation's truth underlies the warning that is later disregarded.
It explicitly contrasts a worldly punishment with the greater punishment of the hereafter.
The fire is named as an everlasting abode and recompense for rejecting signs.
The ordering of affairs across a vast day does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Turning away from remembrance results in being driven into a severe ascending punishment.
Forgetting the Day of Reckoning is explicitly tied to severe punishment.
Mockery becomes a distraction that causes people to forget divine remembrance.
The accusation that Moses forgot is a remote and contextually different use of forgetting.
Forgetting a commanded share produces lasting alienation and future disclosure of deeds.
Hidden reward for deeds is a same-surah contrast without a close link to the focus sequence.
Those addressed acknowledge that they will indeed taste the foretold consequence.
The tree of immortality presents a deceptive aspiration that contrasts with enduring punishment.
It promises severe tasted punishment and repayment for the worst of their deeds.
Denial of the Hour after receiving mercy culminates in being informed of deeds and tasting severe punishment.
The promised eternal garden provides a clear reward-side contrast to everlasting punishment.
The same-surah's revelation is given to warn an unwarned people toward guidance.
Painful punishment and choking food offer a limited sensory parallel to tasting punishment.
The announced punishment is explicitly irreversible, reinforcing finality of the outcome.
The nearby sinners acknowledge seeing and hearing at their Lord, then seek an impossible return.
The announcement of painful punishment is a general warning parallel.
Hope for meeting the Lord is tied to righteous work, positively contrasting the focus ayah's deeds.
Abandoning prayer and following desire ends in meeting ruin.
Forgetting oneself while teaching others is only a distant ethical parallel to neglected encounter.
Remembering generosity in divorce law does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The same-surah call to remember God supplies only broad contextual resonance.
Certainty of meeting and return to God shows the constructive orientation opposed to neglecting it.
The bare claim that revelation is human speech adds no material connection.
The identity of the inheritors is incomplete here and only remotely anticipates enduring reward.
It directly commands disbelievers to taste punishment and names the fire's punishment.
Calling revelation inherited magic is a remote form of rejection without the focus consequences.
Permanent residence in Paradise provides a clear reward-side contrast to permanent punishment.
Forgetting God is answered by God forgetting them, closely paralleling reciprocal abandonment.
Appeal to ancestral custom implies resistance to warning but remains too general.
Taste, trial, death, and return to God provide a broad eschatological framework.
After rejecting warning, the offenders are commanded to taste punishment and warnings.
Calling the signs manifest magic is a general denial with no developed consequence.
The denial of coolness and drink develops the bodily deprivation side of punishment.
It names both Hell and burning punishment for those who persecute believers without repenting.
Mutual waiting only faintly echoes the focus ayah's challenge and eventual consequence.
The imperative to taste introduces an unceasing increase in punishment.
Its distinct question of forgotten or replaced signs offers only a lexical echo.
The brief declaration of loss does not clarify the focus ayah.
Human creation from clay is unrelated to the focus themes.
God neither errs nor forgets, clarifying that divine forgetting is not a memory failure.
The warning about selling a covenant cheaply does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
It directly states that the audience will taste the painful punishment.
Rejection of truth is followed by the arrival of the news they mocked.
Long enjoyment leads people to forget remembrance and become ruined.
The detailed nursing and maintenance ruling is unrelated to the focus ayah.
Forgetting God results in self-forgetting, a close reciprocal-abandonment parallel.
It directly rebukes those who hasten the divine punishment.
Punishment overtakes a warned people, functioning as a confirming sign after rejection.
The assurance concerning mockers does not clarify the focus ayah's themes.
Those who hastened the outcome are commanded to taste the trial they demanded.
It explicitly describes the loss of those who deny meeting God when the Hour arrives suddenly.
The gathered jinn and humans are assigned the Fire as an abiding destination.
It states that those who reject the signs are companions of the Fire, remaining there.
Those who do not expect meeting God are content with worldly life and heedless of His signs.
The Day of gathering makes prior worldly life seem brief and exposes mutual recognition.
It depicts Hell and an imposed, painful drink as a sensory form of punishment.
The condemned person struggles to swallow the drink while death approaches from every side.
Hell's blaze is repeatedly increased for those gathered blind, mute, and deaf.
It directly joins disbelief in God's signs with disbelief in meeting Him and the nullification of deeds.
Hell is assigned as recompense for treating the signs and messengers with mockery.
The heedless and unbelieving are warned of the Day of Regret when the matter is decided.
Turning from divine remembrance brings a constricted life and later resurrection in blindness.
Excess and disbelief in divine signs receive a punishment that is more severe and enduring.
Nearness of account is set against people remaining heedless and turned away.
The scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection establish exact accountability for every deed.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell.
Fire scorches the faces of its inhabitants, making the punishment physically immediate.
The condemned acknowledge that misery overcame them and led them astray.
Their exclusion from divine address gives finality to the punishment after their plea.
Punishment is multiplied and the offender remains therein humiliated.
Hope for meeting God is tied to the certainty that His appointed term will come.
Disbelief in God's signs and meeting Him is joined to despair of mercy and painful punishment.
Reflection on creation is followed by the observation that many people deny meeting their Lord.
The evil end belongs to those who denied and mocked God's signs.
The denial of a new creation after being lost in the earth is explicitly called denial of meeting their Lord.
Death is followed by return to the Lord, supplying the transition into the meeting denied in 32:10.
It states the divine resolve to fill Hell with jinn and humans.
It is the immediate same-surah parallel: the people of the Fire are told to taste the punishment they denied.
Turning away after being reminded of divine signs is answered with certain retribution.
The disbelievers remain in the fire, with neither death nor relief from its punishment.
The promised Hell is identified directly for those who had been warned.
The command to burn in Hell is explicitly grounded in prior disbelief.
Wrongdoers would offer every earthly possession to escape the evil punishment of the Day.
The regret of neglecting duty toward God provides a direct counterpoint to culpable forgetting.
The inhabitants of the Fire dispute while the weak acknowledge following the arrogant into punishment.
The arrogant concede that all are in the Fire and that God has judged between His servants.
The inhabitants of Fire ask its keepers for even a single day of relief from punishment.
God's enemies are gathered to the Fire in ordered groups for judgment.
At arrival, hearing, sight, and skin bear witness to what the condemned used to do.
The body witnesses against its owner, making accountability for deeds unavoidable.
Neither endurance in the Fire nor a plea for restoration offers an escape.
Wrongdoers are shown exposed to the Fire in humiliation, recognizing their true loss.
The command to seize and drag the guilty person into Hell makes punishment concrete and unavoidable.
Pouring boiling punishment over the head gives a direct sensory parallel to tasting punishment.
The taunt directed at the condemned reverses prior claims of honor and power.
The punishment is identified as the reality that had been doubted.
It explicitly says the meeting of this Day was forgotten and answers that neglect with being forgotten.
Those absorbed in worldly enjoyments are commanded to taste humiliating punishment for arrogance and disobedience.
Removal of the veil on the Day makes previously ignored reality sharply visible.
The condemned are driven violently toward the Fire of Hell.
The Fire is identified as the very reality they had denied.
The command to enter and endure the Fire makes it recompense for what they used to do.
Those who went astray and denied are addressed as the recipients of the coming punishment.
Their food from the tree of Zaqqqum makes punishment bodily and sustained.
They drink scalding water after the punishing food, extending its sensory force.
This punitive hospitality is explicitly assigned to the Day of Recompense.
Disbelievers in their Lord receive the punishment of Hell as an evil destination.
The Fire's violent sound and seething depict the force of the punishment awaiting them.
The inhabitants admit that warning came but was denied and rejected.
They confess their sin and acknowledge their exclusion among the companions of the Blaze.
Receiving the record in the left hand begins the condemned person's account of irreversible loss.
The commands to seize, shackle, and burn show punishment as an enacted judgment.
Entry into the burning fire is ordered directly.
A long chain intensifies the image of enduring punitive confinement.
The divine threat to cast the denier into Saqar names the punitive destination.
The question about Saqar emphasizes its terrifying and inescapable reality.
Saqar neither spares nor leaves its victim untouched.
The count of Saqar's guardians adds setting detail but little explanatory force for the focus ayah.
Hell is described as a place of ambush prepared for transgressors.
The transgressors' return to Hell makes it their appointed destination.
Their stay through ages supports the focus ayah's enduring-punishment dimension.
The guilty are veiled from their Lord on the Day of Judgment, reversing the hoped-for encounter.
They then enter the blazing Fire.
They are told that this is the reality they used to deny.
Turning away and disbelieving is made the condition for the ensuing punishment.
God punishes the one who turns away with the greatest punishment.
Return to God grounds the final accountability behind the punishment.
The final reckoning belongs to God alone.
